chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Is a Reserve Currency and Why It Matters

lessons.title: How India and the RBI Hold and Use Forex Reserves

body.text: In June 1991, India had enough foreign exchange left to cover barely three weeks of imports, and had to airlift gold overseas as collateral just to avoid defaulting. Every dollar the RBI holds today is, in part, a response to that memory.

markDefs.definition: The stock of foreign currency assets, gold, and other reserve assets a country's central bank holds, used to settle international obligations, defend the domestic currency, and provide a buffer against external shocks.

children.text: The first two lessons of this chapter looked at reserve currencies from the issuer's side, what it takes to earn that status and what the issuer gains and gives up. This lesson closes the chapter by looking at the other side of the relationship: how a country that does not issue a reserve currency, India, builds and manages its own
as its own buffer against exactly the kind of dollar-driven shocks covered in Lesson 2.
India's Reserves Journey, From Crisis to War Chest

body.title: India's Forex Reserves, 1991 to Today (Rounded Milestones)

events.title: The Balance of Payments Crisis
events.description: Reserves fell to roughly $1 billion, barely enough for a few weeks of imports. India airlifted about 47 tonnes of gold to the Bank of England and the Union Bank of Switzerland as collateral to secure emergency loans and avoid default.

events.title: Liberalisation and the First Buildup
events.description: Economic reforms, a more open current account, and rising software and services exports helped reserves climb from crisis lows to roughly $38 billion by 2000.

events.title: The Global Financial Crisis
events.description: Reserves, which had climbed to roughly $310 billion, were drawn down as the RBI sold dollars to cushion the rupee against capital outflows, falling to around $252 billion.

events.title: The Taper Tantrum, Covered in Lesson 2
events.description: Reserves dipped as the RBI defended the rupee, before a special FCNR(B) deposit swap window helped rebuild them past $300 billion within months.

events.title: A Record War Chest
events.description: Reserves crossed $500 billion in 2020 and peaked at more than $640 billion in 2021, helped by strong foreign portfolio inflows and a weak global trade backdrop during the pandemic.

events.title: Drawn Down to Defend the Rupee Again
events.description: Aggressive US Federal Reserve rate hikes and the Russia-Ukraine war's commodity price shock pushed the RBI to sell dollars again, and reserves fell to roughly $525-540 billion.

events.title: Rebuilt to Fresh Highs
events.description: Reserves recovered and reached new record levels, broadly in the range of $600 to $670 billion, making India one of the largest reserve holders in the world.

children.text: What's Actually Inside the RBI's Reserve Basket

The RBI's reserves are not a single pile of dollar notes. They are split across four components, published weekly in the RBI's Weekly Statistical Supplement, and the split has been shifting gradually in recent years.

body.caption: The four components of India's forex reserves

cells: The largest slice, held mostly in US Treasuries and other highly rated sovereign bonds, plus deposits with other central banks and the Bank for International Settlements
Physical gold held domestically and abroad; the RBI has been steadily increasing this share, discussed later in this lesson
An IMF-created reserve asset whose value is based on a basket of major currencies, dollar, euro, yuan, yen, and pound
India's own contribution to the IMF's resources that it can draw on relatively freely if needed

children.text: Why the RBI Holds This Much

body.label: Import Cover
body.context: Reserves relative to average monthly imports; a widely used cushion metric that fell to just a few weeks in the 1991 crisis

body.caption: Why a country without a reserve currency still needs large reserves of its own

cells: Enough reserves to keep paying for essential imports, oil above all, even if export earnings or capital inflows dry up suddenly
Dollars the RBI can sell in the market to slow a sharp rupee depreciation during episodes like the 2013 taper tantrum or the 2022 Fed hiking cycle
Assurance to foreign lenders and rating agencies that India can meet its external debt obligations even under stress, which in turn keeps its own borrowing costs lower
A buffer against the kind of sudden stop in capital inflows that forced India to the edge of default in 1991

body.text: The 1991 gold pledge is not just a historical footnote, it is the reason India's reserve policy has been conservative ever since. A country that does not issue the world's reserve currency cannot simply print more of what the rest of the world will accept; it has to earn and hold that buffer itself, well before a crisis arrives, not during one.

children.text: Gold's Comeback in the Reserve Mix

For years, the RBI's gold holdings stayed roughly flat at around 560 tonnes. Starting in the late 2010s and accelerating through the 2020s, the RBI began adding gold steadily, taking its holdings past 800 tonnes. This mirrors a broader trend among emerging market central banks, including China and Russia, of diversifying away from a near-total reliance on the US dollar, partly for portfolio balance and partly as insurance against exactly the kind of sanctions leverage covered in Lesson 2. Gold cannot be frozen or cut off from SWIFT the way a dollar account can.

body.title: You Are the RBI's Reserve Manager
body.scenario: Global oil prices spike sharply after a geopolitical shock, widening India's import bill. At the same time, the US Federal Reserve unexpectedly raises interest rates, and foreign investors start pulling money out of Indian equities and bonds, putting pressure on the rupee.
body.prompt: Using what this lesson covered about India's reserve composition and the reasons the RBI holds reserves, what would you expect the RBI to do in the following weeks, and which part of the reserve basket is most likely to be used first?
body.modelAnswer: The RBI would most likely sell dollars from its Foreign Currency Assets, the largest and most liquid component of reserves, directly in the currency market to slow the rupee's fall and prevent a disorderly depreciation, exactly as it did in 2013 and again in 2022. It might also use tools like the FCNR(B) swap window from 2013 to attract fresh dollar inflows from non-resident Indians. Gold would not be the first tool reached for since selling it is slower and more disruptive; it functions more as a long-term diversification and crisis buffer than a day-to-day intervention tool. Import cover would be watched closely throughout, since a sustained fall toward historically low levels, as in 1991, is the signal that would force much harder policy choices, like rate hikes or import curbs.

body.title: Before You Move to Chapter 2
steps: Look up the RBI's latest weekly statistical supplement and note the current split between Foreign Currency Assets, gold, SDRs, and the Reserve Tranche Position
Note India's current import cover in months, and compare it to the roughly 9 to 10 month range this lesson describes as comfortable
Find the RBI's latest reported gold holdings in tonnes and compare it to the roughly 560 tonne base from the late 2010s

With this chapter's three lessons in mind, reserve currency requirements, the exorbitant privilege, and India's own reserve management, move on to Chapter 2, which goes back in history to the gold standard and the British pound's fall from reserve currency status

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: What was the primary trigger for India's 1991 balance of payments crisis response of airlifting gold overseas as collateral?
options: A sudden collapse in India's gold mining output
Foreign exchange reserves falling to roughly $1 billion, barely a few weeks of import cover
A decision by the IMF to stop lending to India entirely
The RBI wanting to test gold's use as an alternative reserve asset
body.explanation: India's reserves had fallen to roughly $1 billion by June 1991, enough for only a few weeks of imports, forcing the government to pledge around 47 tonnes of gold as collateral for emergency loans. This episode is the reason India has since prioritised building a much larger reserve buffer.

body.text: Reserve levels, import cover figures, reserve composition percentages, and gold holdings in this lesson are presented as rounded, widely cited approximations for teaching purposes, drawn from RBI disclosures that are updated weekly and revised over time. Always check the RBI's current Weekly Statistical Supplement for exact, up-to-date figures before citing them professionally. This lesson is educational content, not investment or policy advice.

points: India's approach to forex reserves is shaped directly by the 1991 balance of payments crisis, when reserves fell to roughly $1 billion and gold had to be airlifted overseas as collateral
The RBI's reserves are split across four components, Foreign Currency Assets, gold, SDRs, and the Reserve Tranche Position with the IMF, with Foreign Currency Assets making up the large majority
Reserves are held mainly for import cover, currency defence, debt servicing confidence, and crisis insurance, all functions a reserve currency issuer like the US does not need in the same way
The RBI has been steadily increasing its gold holdings since the late 2010s, part of a broader trend among emerging market central banks diversifying away from dollar concentration

This closes out Chapter 1's look at what reserve currency status means and who holds reserves; Chapter 2 turns to history, starting with the gold standard and the British pound's decline as the world's reserve currency
